title: Two Sum
statement: Given an array of integers and a target, return the indices of the **two distinct elements** whose sum equals the target. Exactly one valid pair exists.
input: Line 1: n. Line 2: n space-separated integers. Line 3: the target.
output: Two indices i and j (0-based, i < j) separated by a space.
hints: A brute-force double loop is O(n²). Can you remember values you've already seen?
For each value v, check whether target − v was seen before, using a hash map from value to index.
solution: Scan once, storing each value's index in a hash map. For element i, if `target - a[i]` is in the map, print the stored index and i. This is O(n) time and O(n) space, versus O(n²) for checking every pair.

title: Reverse Words
statement: Reverse the order of the words in a sentence. Words are separated by one or more spaces; the output must use single spaces with no leading or trailing spaces.

Reverse the list of words and join with one space.
solution: Split the line into tokens (collapsing repeated spaces), reverse the token list and join with a single space. In-place variants reverse the whole string and then each word.

title: Reverse a Linked List
statement: The values of a singly linked list are given in order. Build the list, reverse it **in place** by re-linking nodes, and print the values of the reversed list.
input: Line 1: n (number of nodes). Line 2: n integers (omitted when n = 0).
output: The reversed values separated by spaces, or `empty` if the list is empty.
hints: Keep three references: previous, current and next.
Point current.next to previous, then advance.
solution: Iterate with `prev = null, cur = head`: save `next = cur.next`, set `cur.next = prev`, move `prev = cur`, `cur = next`. When cur is null, prev is the new head.

title: Queue Using Two Stacks
statement: Implement a FIFO queue using only two stacks. Process the operations and print the result of each `pop`, `peek` and `empty`.
input: Line 1: q (number of operations). Next q lines: `push x`, `pop`, `peek` or `empty`.
output: For each pop/peek, the value (or -1 if the queue is empty); for each empty, `true` or `false`. One result per line.
hints: Use one stack for incoming items and one for outgoing items.
Only move items from the input stack to the output stack when the output stack is empty.
solution: Push onto `in`. For pop/peek, if `out` is empty, pop everything from `in` into `out` (reversing order), then use `out`'s top. Each element moves at most once, giving amortised O(1).

title: Number of Islands
statement: Given a grid of `1` (land) and `0` (water), count the islands. An island is formed by horizontally or vertically adjacent land cells.
input: Line 1: rows and columns. Next lines: each row as a string of 0/1.
output: The number of islands.
hints: Every unvisited land cell starts a new island.
Flood-fill (DFS/BFS) from it to mark the whole island visited.
solution: Scan the grid; when you find a `1`, increment the count and flood-fill all connected land to `0` using an explicit stack or queue (avoids recursion depth issues on large grids).

title: Climbing Stairs
statement: You can climb 1 or 2 steps at a time. In how many distinct ways can you reach the top of a staircase with n steps?
input: A single integer n.
output: The number of distinct ways.
hints: ways(n) depends on ways(n − 1) and ways(n − 2).
It is the Fibonacci sequence; keep only the last two values.
solution: `ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2)` with ways(0) = ways(1) = 1. Iterate keeping two variables; use 64-bit integers (n = 80 exceeds 32 bits).

title: Sliding Window Maximum
statement: For every window of size k sliding from left to right over the array, output the maximum value in the window.
input: Line 1: n and k. Line 2: n integers.
output: The n − k + 1 window maxima separated by spaces.
hints: Recomputing each window's max is O(n·k).
Keep a deque of indices whose values are decreasing; the front is the window max.
solution: Maintain a monotonic deque of indices: pop from the back while the new value is ≥ the back's value, push the index, drop the front when it leaves the window. Each index is pushed and popped once.

title: Shortest Paths from a Source
statement: Given an undirected weighted graph with non-negative weights, print the shortest distance from node 1 to every node (1..n), or -1 if unreachable.
input: Line 1: n and m. Next m lines: `u v w` edges.
output: n distances separated by spaces.
hints: BFS works only for unweighted graphs.
Use Dijkstra's algorithm with a min-priority queue; skip stale queue entries.
solution: Dijkstra: initialise dist[1] = 0 and push (0, 1). Pop the smallest distance; skip if it is stale; relax neighbours and push improved distances. Non-negative weights make the greedy choice correct.

title: Second Highest Salary (SQL)
statement: Table `Employees(Id, Name, Salary, DepartmentId)`. Write a query returning the **second highest distinct salary** as a single value. Return NULL when it does not exist.
input: The Employees table (populated per test case).
output: One row with one column: the salary or NULL.
hints: Find the maximum salary below the overall maximum.
Aggregates return NULL over an empty set — use that.
solution: `SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM Employees WHERE Salary < (SELECT MAX(Salary) FROM Employees);` — MAX over no rows yields NULL. A DENSE_RANK() = 2 subquery wrapped in MAX also works.

title: Customers Without Orders (SQL)
statement: Tables `Customers(Id, Name)` and `Orders(Id, CustomerId, Total)`. Return the names of customers who have never placed an order, sorted by name.
input: The Customers and Orders tables.
output: One name per row, sorted ascending.
constraints: Orders.CustomerId may be NULL for guest orders.
hints: Think anti-join.
NOT IN breaks when the subquery returns NULL — prefer NOT EXISTS or LEFT JOIN … IS NULL.
solution: `SELECT c.Name FROM Customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Orders o WHERE o.CustomerId = c.Id) ORDER BY c.Name;` — NOT EXISTS is NULL-safe, unlike NOT IN.

title: Top Earner per Department (SQL)
statement: Tables `Employees(Id, Name, Salary, DepartmentId)` and `Departments(Id, Name)`. For every department, return `DepartmentName|EmployeeName|Salary` for the employee(s) with the highest salary in that department. Sort by department name, then employee name.
input: The Employees and Departments tables.
output: Rows formatted as Department|Employee|Salary.
hints: Rank employees within each department.
RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY DepartmentId ORDER BY Salary DESC) = 1 keeps ties.
solution: Use a window function in a CTE: `WITH r AS (SELECT e.*, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY DepartmentId ORDER BY Salary DESC) rk FROM Employees e) SELECT d.Name, r.Name, r.Salary FROM r JOIN Departments d ON d.Id = r.DepartmentId WHERE rk = 1 ORDER BY d.Name, r.Name;`
